https://www.dw.com/en/german-court-convi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J16P The case was heard at the higher regional court in Stuttgart Image: Joko/imageBROKER/picture alliance Advertisement A German court has sentenced a 30-year-old Ukrainian man to one year and three months in prison over a Russian plot to carry out acts of sabotage . Two other Ukrainian men, aged 22 and 25, were acquitted. The higher regional court in the city of Stuttgart said the three were involved in sending packages with GPS trackers from Germany to Ukraine using a Ukrainian parcel service. According to prosecutors, the aim was to reveal the precise transport routes and pass the information on to Russian secret services. In a second step, prosecutors said the men were planning to dispatch packages designed "to ignite in Germany or elsewhere en route to parts of Ukraine not occupied by Russia and cause as much damage as possible in order to undermine the population's sense of security." However, the plan was discovered before it could be implemented. Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Spying for the purpose of sabotage The three men were arrested in May last year . The 30-year-old who was given jail time "intentionally participated in scouting potential sabotage targets for a Russian state entity," the court said. He was found guilty of "spying for the purposes of sabotage." The court said he involved the other two defendants in the shipment of GPS trackers. However, it could not be proven that those two suspects knew their actions were part of a sabotage plot. The prosecution called for sentences ranging from two years and nine months to four years and three months, while the defense argued for acquittal for all three defendants. Both ​the convicted defendant and the prosecutors have the right to appeal. The enemy within: Ukrainian teenagers recruited by Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Why might Germany be a target? Germany is Ukraine's most important supporter in the war with Russia and has been on high alert for suspected sabotage and spying operations coordinated by Moscow. In a previous case, a series of exploding parcels were shipped from Lithuania in 2024 and detonated in Germany, Poland and Britain. Security sources blamed Russia, although Moscow has denied involvement in such operations. An explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport earlier in August Image: Sebastian Willnow/dpa/picture alliance Earlier this month, a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at eastern Germany's Leipzig Airport, a key military equipment hub. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described it as a "hybrid" attack by a "foreign power" but did not name Russia. Moscow has dismissed suggestions that it was responsible. https://nineoclock.ro/new-registration-d.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount The Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship and Tourism (MEDAT) issued Order no. 1132/16.07.2026, which establishes, by derogation from the provisions of the de minimis aid scheme for the participation of tourism companies in international exhibition events , a single and early deadline for submitting the documentation for participation in three international tourism exhibition events with a business-to-business (B2B) profile. Thus, economic operators interested in participating in Romania’s national stand at the TTG Travel Experience – Rimini (14–16 October 2026), World Travel Market – London (3–5 November 2026) and IBTM World – Barcelona (17–19 November 2026) have the opportunity to submit their participation documentation until 31 July 2026, inclusive. The measure was adopted considering the specifics of these exhibition events, which take place in a predominantly B2B format, participation in them being determinedly conditioned by the use of official digital matchmaking platforms made available by the organizers. Through these platforms, exhibitors create their participation profiles, identify potential business partners and schedule, prior to the official opening of the events, meetings with tour operators, travel agencies, buyers and other international partners in the field. The establishment of an early deadline for submitting documentation allows MEDAT to complete, at a stage prior to the events, the verification and selection process of the participating economic operators, to send the final list of co-exhibitors to the international organizers and to ensure their access to matchmaking platforms starting with the opening period of the business meeting scheduling sessions. The adoption of this measure aims to create optimal conditions for capitalizing on the B2B component of the mentioned exhibition events, to increase the number and quality of scheduled business meetings, as well as to strengthen the opportunities for promoting and developing commercial relations for the tourism industry in Romania. In the absence of that derogation, the general deadline laid down by the de minimis aid scheme would have allowed the documentation to be submitted no later than 30 days before the start of each exhibition event, which would have significantly reduced the time available for accessing matchmaking platforms and scheduling business meetings.ms Source The Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship and Tourism (MEDAT) The diplomatic daily newspaper Nine O’Clock does not assume responsibility for the information received and published on the public website. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e.text: Image source, Getty Images By Liv McMahon Technology reporter Published 1 hour ago Grindr has agreed to pay Â£26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties. The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information. The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants. According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two Â£13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability. Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun. The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission , external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September. "While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing. The firm has agreed to pay Â£13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further Â£13m by 31 March 2027. 'Significant distress' The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws. It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users. People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices. Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent. She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new owners Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data. The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users. It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers. Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards â but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies. It was fined Â£5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices. The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community". "Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.
